                           PROPOSAL FOR DECISION

I.    INTRODUCTION

      Oncor Electric Delivery Company LLC (Oncor) and LCRA Transmission
Services Corporation (LCRA) (collectively, Applicants) filed a joint application
(Application) with the Public Utility Commission of Texas (Commission) to amend
their certificates of convenience and necessity (CCNs) to construct, own, and
operate a proposed Bell County East-to-Big Hill 765-kilovolt (kV) transmission line.
                                             1
                                   Proposal for Decision
                     SOAH Docket No. 473-26-16349, PUC Docket No. 59475
 The transmission line would span Bell, Burnet, Concho, Coryell, Lampasas, Llano,
Mason, Mills, San Saba, Schleicher, Tom Green, and Williamson Counties (the Bell
County East-to-Big Hill Project or Project). The Bell County East-to-Big Hill Project
is one of five extra-high-voltage transmission lines designated in the Permian Basin
Reliability Plan (PBRP) that was developed by the Electric Reliability Council of
Texas (ERCOT) and approved by the Commission. 1


           The PBRP identified a need for additional transmission capacity to serve
forecasted electrical load in the Permian Basin region, which is being driven by oil
and gas development, data centers, crypto mining, and other types of large loads.2
The 2022 Electrification of the Permian Basin study—on which ERCOT relied for its
oil and gas forecasted load growth—reports that major Permian Basin oil and gas
producers are shifting operations that traditionally required non-grid power (such as
gas lift, drilling and completion) to the electrical grid in order to meet strategic
corporate targets, including emissions reductions. According to the 2022 study, this
redirection will significantly increase the oil and gas sector’s demand for electric load
in the Permian Basin. 3

            ERCOT outlined proposed transmission projects in the PBRP to meet this
forecasted demand. After the Commission approved the PBRP, it authorized
transmission service providers—including Oncor and LCRA—to pursue CCN
authorization for five 765-kV transmission lines. 4 The lines make up three 765-kV
“import paths” designed to transfer large-scale power from other regions of the state
into the Permian Basin. These projects would represent one of the largest single
investments in transmission infrastructure in Texas, extending across the western
and central parts of the state. In 2024, ERCOT estimated the total cost at
$13.77 billion. 5 The cost estimate per transmission line mile has risen though: from
$6.2 million to roughly $7.5 million, a 21% increase, and tariff exposure on steel and
aluminum has not been analyzed. 6 A recent economic assessment estimates the
proposed 765-kV transmission buildout would impose nearly $100 billion in lifetime
costs on Texas ratepayers. 7 At the same time, thousands of Texas landowners may
face permanent impacts from new transmission corridors as new rights-of-way
(ROW) are acquired through voluntary easements or eminent domain. The map
below (import paths labeled) shows the location of the three proposed Permian Basin
765-kV transmission import paths. 8

            No 765-kV transmission line has been constructed in Texas. These would be
the first. The proposed 765-kV transmission lines would be constructed on single-
circuit self-supporting steel lattice towers, generally within a 200-foot ROW—
two-thirds the length of a standard American football field from goal line to goal line.
The typical structure would be 140 to 170 feet in height, with a maximum anticipated
height of 198 feet. 9 A building that is 140 to 170 feet tall is a 10-to-14 story structure. 10
A building that is 198 feet tall is 14 to 17 stories. A diagram of a proposed 765-kV steel
lattice tangent tower is part of the Application; it is below. 11

            Oncor and LCRA would construct, own, and operate the two 765-kV
transmission lines that are Import Path 2. The eastern part of Import Path 2 is the
Bell County East-to-Big Hill Project at issue in this case. The length of the proposed
transmission line is 214 to 244 miles, depending on the route. 12 The Project is
between Oncor’s existing Bell County East switch, located 5.5 miles southeast of the
City of Temple in Bell County, and LCRA’s existing Big Hill substation, located
13 miles northeast of the City of Eldorado in Schleicher County. 13 The estimated
costs for the transmission line range from $1.6 billion to almost $1.9 billion plus
$395 million in station costs for work at Oncor’s Bell County East switch. 14

           Import Path 2’s western half is the proposed Big Hill-to-Sand Lake 765-kV
transmission line. The Big Hill-to-Sand Lake Project (Docket No. 59182) extends
across Crane, Crockett, Irion, Pecos, Reeves, Schleicher, Tom Green, Upton, and
Ward Counties, with a proposed line length of 197 to 222 miles depending on the
route. The estimated cost for the Big Hill-to-Sand Lake line is between $976 million
and $1.3 billion plus an estimated $728 million for the substation facilities. 15 The two
Projects share a common point of interconnection at the Big Hill substation.
Docket No. 59182 addresses the Big Hill-to-Sand Lake Project, in part. It is in part,
because the decision on the issue of need for the Big Hill-to-Sand Lake Project is
consolidated with this proceeding, Docket No. 59475.16 Thus, the need for the
entirety of Import Path 2 is being determined in this proceeding.

 The five dockets were filed with the Commission in a west to east sequence, i.e., the
western half of Import Path 1 was filed first, followed by the western half of
Import Path 2, then the eastern half of Import Path 1 was filed, followed by
Import Path 3 (addressed west to east in a single docket), and finally by the eastern

        On June 17, 2026, the Commission considered a motion by Intervenor
American Stewards of Liberty, filed in the five pending 765-kV transmission line
dockets.17 The motion requested the Commission to defer a determination of the
need for any given 765-kV transmission line until a proposal for decision in the fifth
case (i.e., the instant Docket No. 59475) is before the Commission. Although the
Commission did not address the motion to defer a determination of need, it abated
Docket No. 59029—the eastern half of Import Path 1—pending the issuance of the
proposal for decision in Docket No. 59315—the western half of Import Path 1. 18


        After considering the evidence and applicable law, the State Office of
Administrative Hearings (SOAH) Administrative Law Judges (ALJs) recommend
that Oncor and LCRA’s applications for the proposed Bell County East-to-Big Hill
Project and the Big Hill-to-Sand Lake Project be denied. Applicants failed to establish
that the Projects are necessary for the service, accommodation, convenience, or

the ALJs’ denial recommendations and instead proceed with approving the
Applications to amend Applicants’ CCNs, the ALJs provide a routing analysis and
recommendation in this proposal for decision.


II.        JURISDICTION

           The Commission has jurisdiction over the instant Application and Oncor and
LCRA’s application to amend their respective CCNs for the Big Hill-to Sand Lake
Project (Docket No. 59182). The Commission’s jurisdiction and authority is found
in PURA §§ 14.001, 32.001, 37.051, 37.053, and 37.056 and Rule 25.101. SOAH has
jurisdiction to conduct a hearing and render a proposal for decision on both
applications under PURA § 14.053 and Texas Government Code § 2003.049.


III.       PROCEDURAL HISTORY

           The Commission opened this docket on March 6, 2026, and Applicants’
Application was filed 20 days later on March 26. This case is subject to the 180-day
deadline in PURA § 37.057. It requires the Commission to issue a final order on the
Application not later than the 180th day after its filing. In this docket, that date is

 September 22, 2026.21 PURA § 37.057 provides no exception or opportunity for
extension. If the Commission does not meet the deadline, “a party may seek a writ
of mandamus in a district court of Travis County to compel the [C]ommission to
decide on the application.”22 Applicants could have waived the right to mandamus
under PURA § 37.057, effectively extending the statutory deadline, 23 but that did not
happen in this case.


           The Commission’s Order of Referral in this case requires SOAH to issue a
proposal for decision “at least 35 days before the expiration of the 180-day statutory
deadline.” 24 Since neither Applicants nor the Commission offered relief from the
deadline, the ALJs set and adhered to a procedural schedule that would result in a
proposal for decision issued in time for the Commission to issue a final order by
September 22, 2026. As shown in the procedural history below, this resulted in the
case proceeding under a significantly compressed schedule, particularly for an
application of this consequence.

 IV.        APPLICABLE LAW

           An electric utility seeking to obtain or amend a CCN must submit an
application to the Commission. 60 After considering a CCN application for a new
transmission facility, the Commission may take one of three actions: grant the
certificate as requested, grant the certificate for a portion of the facility, or refuse to
grant the certificate. 61 The Commission may grant a certificate “only” if the
Commission finds the transmission facility is necessary for the service,
accommodation, convenience, or safety of the public. 62


           The Commission must consider numerous statutory and regulatory factors
that include:

           (1)     the adequacy of existing service;
           (2)     the need for additional service; and
           (3)     the effect of granting the certificate on the recipient of the certificate
                   and any electric utility serving the proximate area. 63


           In considering the need for additional service for a reliability transmission
project that serves the ERCOT power region, the Commission must consider the
historical load, forecasted load growth, and additional load currently seeking
interconnection, including load for which the electric utility has yet to sign an

            Some of the factors are inherently in conflict, and neither PURA nor
Commission rules specify the relative weight to be given to each factor. The
Commission and the ALJs have the difficult task of considering the totality of all
factors, even if individual factors—when considered in isolation—could lead to
opposite outcomes. The Texas Third Court of Appeals recognized this challenge
when it held: “None of the statutory factors is intended to be absolute in the sense
that any one shall prevail in all possible circumstances. In making these sometimes-
delicate accommodations, the agency is required to exercise its ʻexpertise’ to further
the overall public interest.” 66


           Applicants bear the burden to prove, by a preponderance of the evidence, that
their requested CCN amendment is necessary for the service, accommodation,
convenience, or safety of the public. 67

through one of only two links yet were found reasonable given area constraints. Here,

regulatory constraints. The ALJs determined that 4K Land’s concerns regarding the
use of certain resources and analytical frameworks did not pertain to the adequacy of
alternative routes, and that the Johnson Intervenors’ concerns were more
appropriately addressed at the merits hearing. Thus, the ALJs concluded the
Application provides an adequate number of reasonably differentiated alternative
routes to conduct a proper evaluation and Applicants established facts and
circumstances specific to the study area supporting a reasoned justification for the
routes presented.

            The ALJs’ analysis. Applicants did not meet the requirements of
Rule 22.52(a)(4). Granted, they held “at least one public meeting” before application
filing. But the “at least one” public meeting is a minimum180 tied to “if 25 or more
persons would be entitled to receive direct mail notice of the application.” The 25 or
more persons threshold is embedded in administrative procedure. It is a threshold
that establishes a baseline that proposed action has generated genuine, widespread
controversy or significant stakeholder concern. Thus, for example, a state agency
must grant a public hearing before adoption of a substantive rule if requested by “at
least 25 persons” so that interested persons have a reasonable opportunity “to
submit data, views, or arguments.”181

line is required to send notices and gather community input as part of the planning
process, prior to filing an official application with proposed routes to the PUCT.”

           B.      HOW THE MEASURES ACCUMULATED

          The due-process concern the parties raise, however, is not about one measure
in isolation—it is about their convergence. The measures share a single upstream
cause, the compressed timeline, and they operate in sequence, so their burdens and
deprivations are not independent but cumulative.


          Landowners confronted a near-immediate intervention deadline. Hundreds of
the landowners entered a process in which post-pubic-meeting route additions had
already fixed much of the routing without their input. Many found that, if they
reached the hearing at all, they had literally a few minutes to cross-examine a witness,
with motions for more time denied. And then they had a single week to brief against
a record that closed with 6,399 filings on the Interchange. Each stage narrowed the
opportunity to be heard that the prior stage had already compressed.

I.    INTRODUCTION


      Oncor Electric Delivery Company LLC (Oncor) and LCRA Transmission
Services Corporation (LCRA) (collectively, Applicants) filed a joint application
(Application) with the Public Utility Commission of Texas (Commission) to amend
their certificates of convenience and necessity (CCNs) to construct, own, and
operate a proposed Bell County East-to-Big Hill 765-kilovolt (kV) transmission line.
                                             1
                                   Proposal for Decision
                     SOAH Docket No. 473-26-16349, PUC Docket No. 59475
 The transmission line would span Bell, Burnet, Concho, Coryell, Lampasas, Llano,
Mason, Mills, San Saba, Schleicher, Tom Green, and Williamson Counties (the Bell
County East-to-Big Hill Project or Project). The Bell County East-to-Big Hill Project
is one of five extra-high-voltage transmission lines designated in the Permian Basin
Reliability Plan (PBRP) that was developed by the Electric Reliability Council of
Texas (ERCOT) and approved by the Commission.1


          The PBRP identified a need for additional transmission capacity to serve
forecasted electrical load in the Permian Basin region, which is being driven by oil
and gas development, data centers, crypto mining, and other types of large loads.2
The 2022 Electrification of the Pennian Basin study - on which ERCOT relied for its

oil and gas forecasted load growth-reports that major Permian Basin oil and gas
producers are shifting operations that traditionally required non-grid power (such as
gas lift, drilling and completion) to the electrical grid in order to meet strategic
corporate targets, including emissions reductions. According to the 2022 study, this
redirection will significantly increase the oil and gas sector's demand for electric load
in the Permian Basin.3

          ERCOT outlined proposed transmission projects in the PBRP to meet this

into the Permian Basin. These projects would represent one of the largest single
investments in transmission infrastructure in Texas, extending across the western
and central parts of the state. In 2024, ERCOT estimated the total cost at
$13.77 billion.5 The cost estimate per transmission line mile has risen though: from

proposed 765-kV transmission buildout would impose nearly $100 billion in lifetime
costs on Texas ratepayers.7 At the same time, thousands of Texas landowners may
face permanent impacts from new transmission corridors as new rights-of-way
(ROW) are acquired through voluntary easements or eminent domain. The map
below (import paths labeled) shows the location ofthe three proposed Permian Basin
765-kV transmission import paths.8

 IV.     APPLICABLE LAW


        An electric utility seeking to obtain or amend a CCN must submit an
application to the Commission.6° After considering a CCN application for a new
transmission facility, the Commission may take one of three actions: grant the
certificate as requested, grant the certificate for a portion of the facility, or refuse to
grant the certificate.61 The Commission may grant a certificate "only" if the
Commission finds the transmission facility is necessary for the service,
accommodation, convenience, or safety of the public.62


        The Commission must consider numerous statutory and regulatory factors
that include:

        (1)      the adequacy of existing service;
        (2)      the need for additional service; and
        (3)      the effect of granting the certificate on the recipient of the certificate
                 and any electric utility serving the proximate area. 63


        In considering the need for additional service for a reliability transmission
proj ect that serves the ERCOT power region, the Commission must consider the
historical load, forecasted load growth, and additional load currently seeking
interconnection, including load for which the electric utility has yet to sign an

           Some of the factors are inherently in conflict, and neither PURA nor
Commission rules specify the relative weight to be given to each factor. The
Commission and the ALJs have the difficult task of considering the totality of all
factors, even if individual factors-when considered in isolation-could lead to
opposite outcomes. The Texas Third Court of Appeals recognized this challenge
when it held: "None of the statutory factors is intended to be absolute in the sense
that any one shall prevail in all possible circumstances. In making these sometimes-
delicate accommodations, the agency is required to exercise its 'expertise' to further
the overall public interest. 3)66


          Applicants bear the burden to prove, by a preponderance of the evidence, that
their requested CCN amendment is necessary for the service, accommodation,
convenience, or safety of the public.67

filing. But the "at least one" public meeting is a minimumlso tied to "if 25 or more

that establishes a baseline that proposed action has generated genuine, widespread

must grant a public hearing before adoption of a substantive rule if requested by " at

Texas region's net generation is sufficient to serve Import Path 2.

new and planned gas generation in the Permian Basin-that could reduce or
eliminate the need for Import Path 2, thereby justifying the Commission's

           K.        MODERATION OF IMPACT TO LANDOWNERS


           Pursuant to Rule 25.101(b)(3)(B), a new transmission line must "be routed to
the extent reasonable to moderate the impact on the affected community and
landowners unless grid reliability and security dictate otherwise." In deciding how to
moderate the impact to the community and landowners, the ALJs considered the
other routing factors.


           L.        RouTING RECOMMENDATION


           The ALJs did not find cost to be a distinguishing factor in selecting a route,
since the range of costs for the routes was in a relatively tight range. Similarly, the
lengths among the Focus Routes are also comparable.


           Ultimately, every Focus Route has its advantages and disadvantages. While
Routes 296 and 392 perform favorably on environmental considerations because they
utilize a Colorado River crossing with a pre-existing infrastructure corridor, they each
have considerable downsides. The centerline of Route 296 runs within 500 feet of
Florence Elementary School and two churches. Route 392 has notably more
habitable structures and cultural resources on it than other Focus Routes. As such,
the ALJs find that Routes 487 and 894 achieve prudent avoidance more effectively
than Routes 296 and 392.

XI.   SUMMARY

      Having weighed the credible evidence and arguments of the parties, the AUS
conclude Applicants have not established that the amendment of Applicants' CCNs
is necessary for the service, accommodation, convenience, or safety of the public.
The Bell County East-to-Big Hill and Big Hill-to-Sand Lake Projects should not be
approved. Further, the Application should be denied for Applicants' failure to
comply with the process due to approximately 1,400 landowners under
Rule 22.52(a)(4) for public meeting. Should the Commission determine otherwise,
then Route 894 should be selected for the 765-kV transmission line for the portion of
Import Path 2 at issue in this proceeding. In support of these conclusions, the AUS
make the following findings of fact, conclusions of law, and proposed ordering
paragraphs.

 Need for Import Path 2

                 HB 5066 and the Permian Basin Reliability Plan

68.    In 2023, the 88th Texas Legislature enacted House Bill (HB) 5066, which
       required the Commission and ERCOT to develop a reliability plan for the
       Permian Basin to: (1) extend transmission service to areas where mineral
       resources have been found; (2) increase available capacity to meet forecasted
       load; and (3) provide available infrastructure to reduce interconnection times
       in areas without access to transmission service.

69.    PURA § 37.056(c-1) was amended by the Texas Legislature in 2021 to require
       the Commission, when assessing the need for a reliability project, to "consider
       the historical load, forecasted load growth, and additional load currently
       seeking interconnection." Then, by HB 5066, the section was amended to
       further state that additional load currently seeking interconnection includes
       "load for which the electric utility has yet to sign an interconnection
       agreement, as determined by the electric utility with the responsibility for
       serving the load."

70.    On December 14, 2023, the Commission ordered ERCOT to develop and file
       a Permian Basin reliability plan for the Commission's consideration. For the
       development of the Permian Basin reliability plan, the Commission opened
       Project No. 55718, which had 113 filings on the Commission's Interchange
       prior to the Application being filed.

71 .   Project No . 55718 ' s third filing is the 2022 Electrification of the Pennian Basin
       study (the S&P Global study). This study, prepared for major oil and gas
       companies, was submitted by Oncor to ERCOT. Chevron, ConocoPhillips,
       Devon Energy, Diamondback Energy, ExxonMobil, and Pioneer Natural
       Resources engaged S&P Global to prepare the study. The S&P Global study is
       a follow up to an earlier report that was commissioned by Oncor.

72.    In January 2024, ERCOT began development of a reliability plan for the
       Permian Basin. Over the next six months, ERCOT conducted engineering
       analysis and obtained input from transmission service providers and others in
       the ERCOT region through three meetings of its Regional Planning Group
       (RPG).

                                  The Forecasted Loads

87.   After the PBRP was approved by the Commission, ERCOT adopted an
      adjusted load-forecasting methodology that reduced officer-letter-confirmed
      load from transmission service providers to 55.4% of forecasted MW and
      reduced data center load to 49.8% of forecasted MW. ERCOT's adjusted load-
      forecasting methodology was based on historical analysis of large load
      realization rates.

88.   On April 8, 2025, ERCOT's Board approved the adjusted load-forecasting
      methodology. Then, on May 1, 2025, ERCOT filed a Good Cause Exception
      request with the Commission to adjust the loads for submitted officer-letter-
      attestations and data centers.

89.   By a June 5,2025 order, the Commission directed a discount rate of 55.4% for
      officer-letter loads and 49.8% for data center loads. For any officer-letter loads
      that are data centers, this was a combined discount to adjust that load to 27.6%
      ofthe submitted value. The Commission found: "Good cause exists due to the
      recent actual experience in the ERCOT Region of previously forecasted loads
      coming into service at lower megawatt level than initially claimed and the
      reasonableness of the level of adjustment made by ERCOT to the
      Substantiated Load to account for this."

90.   In the 2025 Regional Transmission Plan (2025 RTP), ERCOT's adjusted load-
      forecasting resulted in a forecasted summer peak demand for 2031 to exceed
      218 GW adjusted to a 2031 forecast of 159 GW: a 27% reduction.

91.   The PBRP load forecast-where 55% of the non-oil and gas load was based on
      officer-confirmed letters, 6% was unconfirmed, and 6% was data centers-has
      not been subjected to or retested against ERCOT's adjusted methodology for
      validating those loads.

92.   Applying ERCOT's adjusted load forecasting to the PBRP non-oil and gas
      projections would result in a material reduction to the forecasted non-oil and
      gas load of at least 3,571 MW, undermining the need for Import Path 2.

93.   Import Path 2's safe loading limit is 5,270 MW

 94.   ERCOT's 2025 RTP estimates large loads-system wide-as follows: data
      center load at 55% of the total growth, hydrogen/ammonia load at 16%,

      load at 7%.

95.   It is material that 59% of the PBRP non-oil and gas load is projected to serve
      cryptocurrency mining-some 6,900 MW. But as set forth in the 2025 RTP,
      there has been a shift in relative share system-wide between crypto and data
      center load. A project designed to serve 6,900 MW of crypto load is not
      automatically the correct project to serve a materially different load mix of
      equivalent nominal size.

96.   After the PBRP was approved by the Commission, the 89th Texas Legislature
      enacted Senate Bill 6 (SB 6), which took effect on June 20, 2025. SB 6 was
      passed to address the risk of large-load interconnection requests (75 MW at a
      single site) might not materialize, while still supporting the state's economic
      growth, while minimizing the potential for stranded infrastructure costs and
      maintaining system reliability. In balancing economic growth and consumer
      interests, the Legislature directed the Commission to establish standards for:

            • uniform financial commitments for large load customers, including
              security on a dollar-per-MW basis or contribution in aid of
              construction;
            • a flat study fee of at least $100,000 for initial transmission screening
                studies;
            •   a method for a large load customer to demonstrate site control;
            • disclosure of whether a large load customer is pursuing similar
              service requests elsewhere in the state; and
            • disclosure by large load customers of on-site backup generating
              facilities to ERCOT.

97.   The PBRP's load forecasts predate these new credibility standards for large
      load interconnections demanded by SB 6.

98.   The Commission has proposed a new rule to implement SB 6-Large Load
      Interconnection Standards (Rule 25.194), but it has not yet been adopted.

104. The S&P Global study identified the driver behind its forecast of surge in
